title: Chapter 7 — Connection Of Civil And Political Associations
paragraphs: There is only one country on the face of the earth where citizens enjoy unlimited freedom of association for political purposes. This same country is the only one in the world where the continual exercise of the right of association has been brought into civil life as well, and where all the advantages civilization can confer are obtained through it. In every country where political associations are prohibited, civil associations are rare. It is hardly likely that this is the result of chance. The inference should rather be that there is a natural, and perhaps a necessary, connection between these two kinds of associations. Some men happen to share a common interest in some concern — a commercial venture to be managed, some manufacturing speculation to be tried; they meet, they combine, and in this way they gradually become familiar with the principle of association. The greater the variety of small affairs, the more men acquire, even without knowing it, the facility for carrying on great undertakings together. Civil associations, then, make political association easier. But conversely, political association remarkably strengthens and improves associations for civil purposes. In civil life every man may, strictly speaking, imagine he can provide for his own needs; in politics he can imagine no such thing. When a people, then, has any knowledge of public life, the idea of association and the wish to unite present themselves every day to the whole community. Whatever natural reluctance may restrain men from acting in concert, they will always be ready to combine for the sake of a party. So political life makes the love and practice of association more general; it arouses a desire for union and teaches the means of combination to numbers of men who would otherwise have always lived apart.

Politics gives rise not only to numerous associations but to associations on a large scale. In civil life it seldom happens that any single interest brings a very large number of men to act together; much skill is required to bring such an interest into being. But in politics, opportunities arise every day. It is only in large associations, however, that the full value of the principle of association is displayed. Citizens who are individually powerless do not clearly see the strength they can acquire by uniting; it has to be shown to them before they understand. It is often easier, therefore, to gather a multitude for a public purpose than to gather a few people for a private one. A thousand citizens do not see what interest they have in combining; ten thousand will see it perfectly clearly. In politics men combine for great undertakings, and the use they make of the principle of association in important affairs teaches them, in practice, that it is their interest to help each other in lesser ones. A political association at once draws a number of individuals out of their own circle. However they may naturally be kept apart by age, temperament, or fortune, it brings them closer together and into contact. Once they have met, they can always meet again.

Men can enter few civil partnerships without putting a share of their possessions at risk; this is so with all manufacturing and trading companies. When men are still little versed in the art of association and unfamiliar with its main rules, they are afraid, the first time they combine in this way, of paying dearly for their experience. They therefore prefer to deprive themselves of a powerful instrument of success rather than run the risks it involves. They are, however, less reluctant to join political associations, which appear to them to be without danger because they stake no money in them. But they cannot belong to such associations for any length of time without discovering how order is maintained among a large number of men, and by what contrivance they are brought to move, harmoniously and methodically, toward the same object. So they learn to surrender their own will to that of all the rest, and to make their own efforts subordinate to the common impulse — things no less necessary to know in civil than in political associations. Political associations can therefore be regarded as large free schools where all the members of the community go to learn the general theory of association.

But even if political association did not directly contribute to the progress of civil association, to destroy the former would be to weaken the latter. When citizens can only meet in public for certain purposes, they regard such meetings as a strange, rare event, and they hardly think about them at all. When they are allowed to meet freely for any purpose, they come to see public association as the universal, and in a way the only, means men can use to accomplish the various purposes they have in mind. Every new need instantly revives the notion. The art of association then becomes, as I have said before, the mother of action — studied and applied by all.

When some kinds of associations are prohibited and others permitted, it is difficult to tell the former from the latter in advance. In this state of uncertainty, men abstain from associations altogether, and a kind of public opinion takes hold that tends to regard any association whatsoever as a bold and almost illicit enterprise.*a

[Footnote a: This is especially true when the executive government has discretionary power to allow or prohibit associations. When certain associations are simply prohibited by law, and the courts of justice have to punish violations of that law, the evil is far less serious. Every citizen then knows beforehand roughly what to expect. He judges himself before he is judged by the law, and, abstaining from prohibited associations, he enters those that are legally sanctioned. It is by such restrictions that all free nations have always admitted the right of association may be limited. But if the legislature were to give a man the power of deciding in advance which associations are dangerous and which are useful, and to authorize him either to destroy all associations in the bud or to let them be formed, then, since no one could foresee in what cases associations might be established and in what cases they would be suppressed, the spirit of association would be entirely paralyzed. The first kind of law would only strike at certain associations; the second would strike at society itself and injure it. I can conceive of a regular government resorting to the first; I do not grant that any government has the right to enact the second.]

It is therefore a fantasy to suppose that the spirit of association, when repressed on one point, will nevertheless display the same vigor on all others, and that if men are allowed to carry on certain undertakings in common, that will be enough to make them eager to do so. When the members of a community are allowed and accustomed to combine for every purpose, they will combine as readily for small purposes as for great ones. But if they are only allowed to combine for small matters, they will be neither inclined nor able to do so. It is in vain to leave them entirely free to carry on their business as joint-stock companies. They will hardly bother to take advantage of the rights you have granted them. And after exhausting your strength in vain efforts to suppress the prohibited associations, you will be surprised that you cannot persuade men to form the associations you encourage.

I do not say that there can be no civil associations in a country where political association is prohibited, for men can never live in society without entering into some common undertakings. But I maintain that in such a country civil associations will always be few in number, feebly conceived, clumsily managed; they will never form any vast designs, or they will fail in carrying them out.

This naturally leads me to think that freedom of association in political matters is not as dangerous to public tranquility as is supposed, and that possibly, after having stirred society up for a time, it may in the end strengthen the state. In democratic countries political associations are, so to speak, the only powerful persons who aspire to rule the state. Accordingly, the governments of our time regard such associations just as sovereigns in the Middle Ages regarded the great vassals of the crown: they feel a kind of instinctive abhorrence of them and combat them on every occasion. They bear, by contrast, a natural goodwill toward civil associations, because they readily notice that, instead of directing the minds of the community to public affairs, such institutions divert them from such reflections. By engaging men more and more in the pursuit of objects that cannot be attained without public tranquility, civil associations deter them from revolutions. But these governments fail to notice that political associations amazingly multiply and facilitate those of a civil character, and that in avoiding a dangerous evil they deprive themselves of an effective remedy.

When you see the Americans freely and constantly forming associations to promote some political principle, to raise one man to the head of affairs or wrest power from another, you have some difficulty understanding how men so independent do not constantly fall into the abuse of freedom. If, on the other hand, you survey the countless trading companies in operation in the United States, and see that the Americans are everywhere ceaselessly engaged in carrying out important and difficult plans which the slightest revolution would throw into confusion, you readily understand why people so well occupied are in no way tempted to disturb the state or to destroy the public tranquility from which they all benefit.

Is it enough to observe these things separately, or should we not look for the hidden tie that connects them? In their political associations, Americans of all conditions, minds, and ages daily acquire a general taste for association and grow accustomed to using it. There they meet in large numbers, they converse, they listen to each other, and they stimulate one another to all kinds of undertakings. Then they carry the notions they have thus acquired over into civil life and put them to a thousand uses. Thus it is by enjoying a dangerous freedom that the Americans learn the art of making the dangers of freedom less formidable.

If a particular moment in the life of a nation is selected, it is easy to show that political associations disturb the state and paralyze productive industry. But take the whole life of a people, and it may perhaps be easy to demonstrate that freedom of association in political matters is favorable to the prosperity and even the tranquility of the community.

I said in the earlier part of this work: "The unrestrained liberty of political association cannot be entirely equated with the liberty of the press. The first is at once less necessary and more dangerous than the second. A nation may confine it within certain limits without ceasing to be its own master, and it may sometimes be obliged to do so in order to maintain its own authority." And further on I added: "It cannot be denied that the unrestrained liberty of association for political purposes is the last degree of liberty a people is fit for. If it does not throw them into anarchy, it perpetually brings them, as it were, to the brink of it." So I do not think a nation is always free to grant its citizens an absolute right of association for political purposes, and I doubt that in any country, in any age, it is wise to set no limits to freedom of association. A certain nation, it is said, could not maintain tranquility in the community, get its laws respected, or establish a lasting government if the right of association were not confined within narrow limits. These blessings are undoubtedly invaluable, and I can imagine that, to acquire or preserve them, a nation may impose on itself severe temporary restrictions. But it is still well for the nation to know at what price these blessings are bought. I can understand that it may be wise to cut off a man's arm to save his life, but it would be ridiculous to claim that he will be as dexterous afterward as he was before he lost it.
